----------------------------------------------------------------
COMPLETE EMPIRICAL RESEARCH PLAN
----------------------------------------------------------------

1. IDENTIFICATION STRATEGY  
Chosen method: Two–stage least squares (2SLS) instrumental-variables design embedded in a difference-in-differences (DiD) framework (“shift-share IV”).  

Why IV is appropriate  
• Theory predicts that family housing wealth—net of income—affects liquidity‐constrained educational investment, but actual home values are endogenous to local economic fundamentals that also influence college‐going (e.g., wages, labor-demand shocks).  
• Geographic dispersion in the late-1990s/early-2000s housing boom produced large, arguably exogenous, cross-area differences in appreciation rates that can be used as instruments.  
• PSID contains the same families over time, allowing us to construct child-level panels of predicted (“exogenous”) housing wealth shocks.  

Implementation  
Stage-1: Predict the change in a household’s housing equity with the interaction of (i) the change in the local FHFA house-price index (HPI) in the child’s MSA between ages 14 and 18 and (ii) an indicator that the family owned a home at age 14.  

ΔPredicted Equity_hi = β₁ ΔHPI_msa × Owner14_hi + β₂X + μ_s + τ_t + ε_hi  

Stage-2: Regress the child’s college enrollment on the fitted values from stage 1, controlling for family income and fixed effects for state and year.  

This is equivalent to a difference-in-differences with three dimensions:  
(1) time (pre- vs post-housing-boom years), (2) geography (places with big vs small HPI growth), (3) homeownership status (owners vs renters).  

2. TREATMENT AND CONTROL  

Treatment variable  
Treated = magnitude of the instrumented change in real housing EQUITY of the child’s family between ages 14 and 18 (continuous).  

Control group / counterfactual  
• Renting families in the same MSA and year provide the main within-area counterfactual because they face the same local labor market but do not receive the housing-wealth shock.  
• Homeowning families in MSAs with little or no price growth act as an additional control.  

Treatment timing / event date  
Event window: four calendar years ending in the spring after the child’s 18th birthday (high-school graduation cohort). HPI changes are cumulated over that window.  

3. KEY IDENTIFYING ASSUMPTIONS  

IV-1. Relevance – Local HPI changes strongly predict changes in individual housing equity for owners. Highly plausible: nationwide evidence shows pass-through from HPI to household equities with elasticities 0.6–0.9.  

IV-2. Exclusion – Conditional on covariates (local unemployment, income, demographics), local HPI moves affect children’s college enrollment ONLY through the induced change in the parents’ housing wealth/liquidity.  
Plausibility: college costs are set nationally, aid formulas exclude home equity, and renters in the same labor market provide a placebo test.  

IV-3. Monotonicity – When HPI rises, no owner’s housing equity falls relative to the counterfactual; when HPI falls, no owner’s equity rises. Reasonable given standard mortgage contracts.  

DiD Common-Trends – In the absence of the housing-wealth shock, enrollment trends for owners and renters (or high- and low-boom MSAs) would have evolved in parallel. Testable in pre-1995 data.  

SUTVA – One family’s housing-wealth shock does not directly affect other families’ college choices (no spillovers). Likely satisfied at the MSA level.  

4. MAJOR THREATS & MITIGATION  

Threat 1: Local labor-demand shocks simultaneously raise wages, housing prices, and opportunity costs of college.  
Mitigation:  
• Control for MSA-year unemployment rate, payroll employment growth, and real per-capita income.  
• Include MSA-specific linear time trends.  
• Placebo on renters: HPI should not predict their college outcomes if labor shocks are fully captured by controls.  

Threat 2: Selective migration—families with college-bound kids might move to booming housing markets.  
Mitigation:  
• Measure ownership status and HPI using the MSA where the family resided when the child was 14 (pre-determined).  
• Drop households that move across MSAs between 14 and 18 in a robustness check.  
• Instrument remains valid if migration is unrelated to unobserved shocks to enrollment conditional on observables.  

Threat 3: Measurement error in self-reported home values biases OLS and weakens first stage.  
Mitigation:  
• HPI-based instrument relies only on reported value at age 14 and aggregate price index changes—measurement error in levels is swept out in differencing and attenuates toward zero, not biasing the IV second stage.  
• Cluster-robust standard errors at the MSA level to account for common shocks.  

5. R CODE OUTLINE  

```r
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# 0. Packages
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
library(data.table)   # fast data handling
library(fixest)       # regression with IV and fixed effects
library(modelsummary) # neat summary tables

# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# 1. Data Loading
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
psid   <- fread("psid_child_cohorts.csv")   # child-level PSID extract
state  <- fread("state_controls.csv")       # unemployment & income
fhfa   <- fread("fhfa_hpi_msa.csv")         # quarterly HPI series

# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# 2. Merge & Construct Variables
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# Collapse FHFA to 4-year growth for each MSA ending at child age 18
fhfa[, hpi_growth := 100 * (log(hpi_qtr) - shift(log(hpi_qtr), 16)),  # 16 quarters = 4 yrs
     by = .(msa)]
fhfa_growth <- fhfa[, .SD[.N], by = .(msa, year)]  # keep year-end obs

# Merge into PSID
dat <- merge(psid, fhfa_growth[, .(msa, year, hpi_growth)],
             by = c("msa","year"), all.x = TRUE)
dat <- merge(dat, state, by = c("state","year"), all.x = TRUE)

# Create homeownership at age 14 indicator
dat[, owner14 := as.integer(homeowner_age14 == 1)]

# Predicted change in housing equity (instrument)
dat[, delta_pred_equity := hpi_growth/100 * home_value_age14 * owner14]

# First-stage endogenous var: actual Δ home equity between 14 and 18
dat[, delta_actual_equity := home_equity_age18 - home_equity_age14]

# Outcome: College Enrollment (1 = >12 yrs schooling by age 20)
dat[, enroll := as.integer(educ_years_by20 > 12)]

# Controls
dat[, log_income := log(real_family_income_age18 + 1)]
controls <- c("log_income", "unemp_rate", "real_pcap_income",
              "hhsize", "black", "hispanic", "female", "parents_educ")

# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# 3. Main Specification (2SLS)
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
iv_formula <- as.formula(paste(
  "enroll ~", paste(controls, collapse = " + "),
  "|",                         # feols IV syntax Y ~ X | Z
  "(delta_actual_equity ~ delta_pred_equity) |", 
  "state^year + msa"           # fixed effects: state-year & MSA
))

est_main <- feols(iv_formula, data = dat, cluster = "msa")

# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# 4. Robustness Check: Owners vs Renters Triple-Diff
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
dat[, treat := owner14 * hpi_growth]  # interaction
est_triple <- feols(
  enroll ~ treat + hpi_growth + owner14 + 
           paste(controls, collapse="+") | state^year + msa,
  data = dat, cluster = "msa"
)

# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# 5. Results Table
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
modelsummary(list(Main_IV = est_main, Triple_Diff = est_triple),
             output = "markdown")
```

6. EXPECTED RESULTS  

Direction: Positive. A $10,000 exogenous increase in home equity between ages 14 and 18 is expected to raise the probability of college enrollment by roughly 2–3 percentage points for families in the bottom half of the income distribution, and by near-zero for the top quartile, reflecting diminishing marginal utility of liquidity.  

Magnitude rationale: Average tuition net of aid at public four-year colleges in early 2000s ≈ \$6–8 k. Liquidity‐constrained households likely operate with marginal propensities to invest in postsecondary education of 0.2–0.3 with respect to unexpected wealth shocks.  

7. VALIDITY CHECKLIST SELF-ASSESSMENT (IV)  
C1 (Relevance of instrument): 1  
C2 (Exclusion/independence): 0.5 (some remaining concerns about local shocks)  
C3 (Monotonicity): 1  
C4 (Common trends / parallel paths for owners vs renters pre-boom): 0.5  
C5 (SUTVA / no spillovers): 1  

TOTAL = 4 / 5 → Overall validity looks good but not bullet-proof; parallel-trend tests and richer local controls remain essential.
